findings.claim: For OCR, you study it as a modern drama text in Component 01 or 02. (Repeated in lesson 8: 'you will typically be asked to write about Leave Taking in Component 01 or 02'.)
findings.truth: Leave Taking is a modern prose or drama set text and is examined in one place only: Section A of the first examined component. The second component is poetry across time plus Shakespeare and never carries this text. Telling a student the play may come up on either paper invites them to prepare for a question that cannot be set.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md, section 3a: 'Exploring modern and literary heritage texts (01) ... Section A: Modern prose or drama ... Learners study one modern prose or drama set text'; the set-text list at line 717 places 'Leave Taking - Winsome Pinnock' in that list only. 'Exploring poetry and Shakespeare (02)' contains only the poetry cluster and the Shakespeare play.

findings.claim: You may receive an extract with accompanying questions, or be asked to write about the whole play. All tasks reward AO1, AO2 and AO3. (Plus 'Extract analysis strategy: Work through the extract methodically ... Quote precisely.')
findings.truth: There is no either/or. The studied text carries ONE question split into two compulsory parts: (a) a comparison of a printed extract from Leave Taking with an unseen, same-genre modern extract, 20 marks; AND (b) a related question on the same studied text, 20 marks - 40 marks in total. The exam is closed text. AO4 (spelling and punctuation) is assessed only in Section B of that component, so this text carries no such marks. The extract strategy also omitted the comparison, which is the whole of part (a).
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md, section 3a: 'Learners respond to one extended response-style question on their studied text, which is split into two parts: a) A comparison of an extract from the studied text with a modern, same-genre unseen extract AND b) A related question on the same studied text'; 'This component is a closed text, 2 hour examination worth 80 marks: 40 marks for Section A and 40 marks for Section B'; section 3h: 'accurate spelling and punctuation (AO4) in Section B of each examined component'.

findings.claim: Enid speaks predominantly in standard English - the language of assimilation ... when she is emotional, stressed or speaking about Jamaica, her language shifts: Jamaican patois breaks through the English surface. (Repeated through lesson 7 content, its knowledge checks, its matching item, two mark schemes, six flashcards and the glossary; also lesson 5: 'she speaks proper English'.)
findings.truth: Enid speaks Jamaican patois throughout the play. Every Enid line in the published study material is in patois: 'I proud a my girls', 'England been good to me', 'I work jobs seven days a week' (Scene 2), 'In a way, we poorer than them' (Scene 8). The irony Pinnock builds is that Enid demands English respectability from her daughters in a voice that never sounds English; it is her London-born daughters who speak English. A student taught the lesson's version would misread every Enid speech and would hunt for 'slippage' moments that do not exist.
findings.evidence: Oak National Academy, 'Enid: England been good to me' (AQA programme) - emphasises Enid's Jamaican patois with the quoted lines; Nick Hern Books GCSE study guide extract for Leave Taking (2024), quoted ENID lines from Scenes 2 and 3. Same finding was raised and fixed on the sibling unit english-literature-aqa/leave-taking (F2 in its report, checked 2 Sep 2026).

findings.claim: Enid's North London living room appears in Scenes 2-5 ... Mai's Deptford bedsit appears in Scenes 1, 6, 7 and 8. Scenes 1-5 are slower, domestic ... Scenes 6-8 accelerate. (Same split in lesson 1 content and its matching knowledge check, a lesson 6 knowledge-check option and three lesson 6 flashcards; lesson 3 also places Viv's exam walkout in Scene 5 without saying where.)
findings.truth: Scene 5 is at Mai's bedsit, not at Enid's. By Scene 5 the action has skipped forward a few weeks, Del is living with Mai, Mai reads Del's palm and identifies her dyslexia, and Viv comes to Mai's to tell Del she has walked out of her English Literature A-level. The correct split is Enid's home = Scenes 2-4, Mai's bedsit = Scenes 1 and 5-8. This also makes the 4/4 pacing split in the same lesson internally consistent.
findings.evidence: WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser for Leave Taking, Scene 5: 'This scene skips forward a few weeks with Del living with Mai ... Viv comes to visit'; Oak National Academy, 'An exploration of Scene Five': 'Scene Five takes place at Mai's home, with Del and Mai present'. Same finding on the sibling AQA unit (F3).

findings.claim: Scene 1 takes place at Mai's Deptford bedsit on Easter Monday. Enid brings both daughters to Mai for a reading - her stated concern is about a letter she received from her sister Cynthia in Jamaica saying that their mother is seriously ill and asking for money ... Enid's other worry - which she shares cautiously - is about Del's behaviour. (Also two flashcards, and a lesson 2 mark scheme listing 'the letter about the mother's illness'.)
findings.truth: The emphasis is reversed and the letter is invented. Enid's stated concern in Scene 1 is Del, who has been staying out late and whom Enid already suspects is pregnant. The money is a secondary thread: Enid tells Mai how hard she finds her sister's constant requests, and Mai advises her to send it anyway. There is no letter saying the mother is seriously ill. No board or publisher source records an Easter Monday setting either, and it reads like a stage direction a student would quote.
findings.evidence: WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, Scene 1: 'Enid is concerned as her eldest daughter, Del, has been staying out late and Enid suspects that she is pregnant'; Nick Hern study guide, Scene Three note: 'Enid's doubts expressed in Scene One about the constant requests for money'. Same finding on the sibling AQA unit (F6, F5).

findings.claim: set in 1984 London (three times in lesson 1, once in lesson 8's exam advice); 'Scene 1 takes place on Easter Monday, 1984'; knowledge check 'In what year is Leave Taking set?' keyed to 1984 with 1987 offered as a wrong answer; flashcard 'London, in 1984.'
findings.truth: The play is set in 1980s London. No board or publisher source gives a year. Nick Hern's own study guide timeline places the action around 1987 and puts Enid's last visit to Jamaica in 1982, in the past. The knowledge check therefore marked a defensible answer (1987) wrong, so it has been repointed to the first-performance year, which is documented.
findings.evidence: Nick Hern Books set-text page for Leave Taking: premiere Liverpool Playhouse Studio 1987, setting given as North London with no year; Bush Theatre 2018 production page (setting Deptford, London, no year); Oak National Academy introduction lesson: 'set in London during the 1980s'. Same finding on the sibling AQA unit (F5).

findings.claim: Mai reads Enid's palm and tells her she will make a long journey. This prediction introduces the possibility of reconciliation that the final scene will deliver. (Flashcard: 'What does Mai predict when she reads Enid's palm in Scene 6?' - 'That Enid will make a long journey.')
findings.truth: There is no palm reading and no long-journey prediction in Scene 6. Enid comes to Mai's, admits her grief and her fear for Del, and lets out a howl of pain. Mai gives her something for the stress but refuses to say where Del is, and answers her with a definition of home - that if you are at peace with yourself you are at home anywhere. After Enid leaves, Mai tells Del she should go back to her mother. The only palm readings in the play are Mai reading Del's (Scene 5), Del reading Mai's (Scene 8) and Del reading Enid's (the closing image).
findings.evidence: WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, Scene 6: 'Mai gives Enid something for the stress but doesn't tell her where Del is. After Enid leaves, Mai tells Del she should return to her mother'; Oak National Academy, 'An exploration of Scene Six'. Same finding on the sibling AQA unit (F7).

findings.claim: Del becomes pregnant during this section of the play [Scenes 4-7] ... Enid's worry about Del in Scene 1 ... is later confirmed.
findings.truth: Del is already in the early stages of pregnancy when the play opens. Enid suspects it in Scene 1 - it is why she takes Del to Mai. The pregnancy becomes open later; it does not begin mid-play. Getting the order wrong weakens any structural argument about Scene 1 as exposition.
findings.evidence: WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, character note: 'Del: Enid's 18-year-old daughter. She is in the early stages of pregnancy'; Scene 1: 'Enid suspects that she is pregnant'. Same finding on the sibling AQA unit (F8).

findings.claim: The news arrives via another letter - confirming what Enid had feared since Scene 1.
findings.truth: The news of the mother's death comes by telephone in Scene 3. Viv answers a call from Enid's sister in Jamaica; the stage direction reads 'As ENID listens something drains out of her. She drops the phone'. The dropped phone is one of the play's best-known stage images, so the lesson removes the very moment a student would quote.
findings.evidence: Nick Hern Books GCSE study guide extract, Scene Three: 'Enid receives a phone call from Cynthia informing her that Mooma has died', with the quoted stage direction; WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, Scene 3: 'Viv answers a phone call from her aunt who rings to tell the family that Enid's mother has died'. Same finding on the sibling AQA unit (F4).

findings.claim: Mai, who is dying, has given Del her notebook ... 'Mai is not simply dying'; 'A half-burnt white candle sits near Mai - her life and role ending'; lesson 4 description 'Mai's departure'; lesson 3 'clearly dying'; lesson 5 'nearly fainting at one point, clearly dying by the end'; flashcards 'What does Mai leave Del as her inheritance?' and 'That her life and her role are ending.'
findings.truth: Mai does not die, and there is no departure. She is unwell - a dizzy spell in Scene 5, and in Scene 8 Del reads her palm, senses a health problem and tells her to see a doctor, which Mai deflects. She hands over the notebook because she has no daughter of her own to pass her knowledge to, not because she is dying. The notebook itself is correct.
findings.evidence: WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, Scene 8: 'Mai giving Del her notebook as she does not have her own daughter to pass her knowledge on to'; Nick Hern study guide, Scene Eight: 'Del detects that Mai may have some health complications, after reading her palm, and tells her that she should go and see a doctor. Mai avoids the conversation'. Same finding on the sibling AQA unit (F11).

findings.claim: Brod ... has lost contact with his children (lesson 2); 'has children he no longer sees' (lesson 5); 'estrangement from his children' (lesson 3 mark scheme).
findings.truth: Brod has a wife and children in Jamaica, whom he visits. He is disenchanted and drinks, but he is not estranged from his family; his ties back home are part of what makes him the play's Caribbean conscience.
findings.evidence: Oak National Academy, 'The presentation of the male characters in Leave Taking': Brod 'has a wife and children in Jamaica whom he visits'. Same finding on the sibling AQA unit (F9).

findings.claim: 'no matter how hard I search for myself in them books, I'm never there.' (lesson 5 content and flashcard; paraphrased in lesson 3 as 'no matter how hard I search for myself in these books').
findings.truth: The line is 'But no matter how much I search for myself in them books, I'm never there' - Viv, Scene 5. 'Hard' for 'much' is a one-word misquotation of the unit's single most quotable line, and lesson 3 offers it only as a paraphrase where a student needs the exact words.
findings.evidence: Quoted as Viv, Scene 5 in the widely used GCSE quotation sets for Leave Taking; same wording established on the sibling AQA unit (F14).

findings.claim: Her mother called her 'Miss English', mocking Enid's assimilation (lesson 2); 'Enid's mother called her Miss English' (lesson 5); flashcard keyed to the mother.
findings.truth: It is her friends and family back in Jamaica, in Scene 3, who call Enid 'Miss English'. Pinning it on her mother alone narrows a community judgement into a private one and mis-sources a quotation a student may use.
findings.evidence: Oak National Academy, 'Enid's relationships with Jamaica and England': 'Enid's friends and family in Jamaica call her Miss English (Scene Three)'. Same finding on the sibling AQA unit (F12).

findings.claim: Enid must face what she has suppressed, Del must choose whether to allow Enid back into her life, and Viv must prepare for her departure to university [in Scene 8].
findings.truth: Viv is not in Scene 8. The scene has only Del, Mai and Enid on stage; Viv's university place is reported by Enid. A student writing about Viv's presence in the final scene would be marked wrong on the text.
findings.evidence: Nick Hern Books GCSE study guide, Scene Eight: 'Who's in it? Del, Mai and Enid'; WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, Scene 8. Same finding on the sibling AQA unit (F13).

findings.claim: She is a first-generation Jamaican immigrant who came to England around 1959 ... (Flashcard: 'Around which year did Enid come to England from Jamaica?' - '1959.')
findings.truth: The play does not date Enid's arrival. 1959 is the year Winsome Pinnock's own mother migrated from Jamaica, which Pinnock gives in an interview about the play's origins - it is the playwright's biography, not the character's. Enid is described only as having come to England as a young woman.
findings.evidence: Winsome Pinnock, 'Reaching out for life in a new country' (Nick Hern Books blog, 23 May 2018): her mother 'migrated from Jamaica to the UK in 1959'; WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser: 'Enid came to England as a young woman having left her family in Jamaica'. Same finding on the sibling AQA unit (F10).

findings.truth: Titles are not editable through _edits.json, so the orchestrator must patch these two. Lesson 2 is titled 'Act 1: Enid, Viv & the Obeah Woman' and lesson 3 'Act 2: Generational Conflict'. The play has eight numbered scenes and no acts. Lesson 6 tells students to say 'Scene 1' and never 'Act 1', and lesson 8 lists 'Referring to Act 1 and Act 2' as a common mistake, so the unit contradicts itself in its own navigation. Lesson 2's title also names the wrong daughter: its own conclusion and exam tip call the lesson 'Scenes 1-3: Enid, Del and the Obeah Woman', and Del, not Viv, is the daughter who stays behind with Mai. Recommended titles: lesson 2 'Scenes 1-3: Enid, Del and the Obeah Woman'; lesson 3 'Scenes 4-7: Crises, Conflict and Revelation' (both taken from the lessons' own conclusion text). ORCHESTRATOR: titles patched via Supabase, see _title_fix.log.
findings.claim: Lesson 2 title 'Act 1: Enid, Viv & the Obeah Woman'; lesson 3 title 'Act 2: Generational Conflict'.
findings.evidence: Nick Hern Books published text is in eight numbered scenes (stated in lesson 6 itself); WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser and Oak National Academy both work scene by scene, Scene One to Scene Eight.

findings.claim: She works as a hospital cleaner - sometimes at two jobs simultaneously (lesson 5); 'as a hospital cleaner, sometimes at two jobs' (lesson 2); flashcard 'A hospital cleaner, sometimes working two jobs at once.'
findings.truth: Enid working two jobs is well attested ('I work jobs seven days a week', Scene 2). 'Hospital cleaner' is not: no board, publisher or Oak resource reached in this pass names her job, and the orchestrator's brief points to nursing instead. Two defensible corrections: (a) if the text gives a nursing or auxiliary post, change all three places to that; (b) if the text names no job, cut the specific title and keep 'She works long hours, sometimes at two jobs'. Option (b) is the safe patch and I recommend it unless someone can check the text. Not edited, because a wrong job title would be no better than the current one. ORCHESTRATOR: no source names the job or settles the marriage; applied the neutral wording (two jobs / the marriage ended).
findings.evidence: Absent from the Nick Hern set-text page, the Bush Theatre 2018 production page, the WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser summary and the Oak lesson titles consulted. Web search was unavailable this session, so this could not be closed.

findings.claim: She was abandoned by her husband after he subjected her to domestic violence (lesson 5) - but lesson 3 says 'Enid eventually left him, but she never told her daughters the truth about why', and a lesson 5 flashcard asks 'How did Enid's husband treat her before she left him?'
findings.truth: The unit contradicts itself about who ended the marriage, and a student could be marked wrong either way. No source reached in this pass settles it. Whoever holds a copy of the play should read Brod's Scene 7 speech and make the two lessons agree; the safe wording if the text is vague is 'the marriage ended', which fits both readings. Not edited, because picking one version without evidence would simply move the error. ORCHESTRATOR: no source names the job or settles the marriage; applied the neutral wording (two jobs / the marriage ended).
findings.evidence: Internal contradiction measured between raw/L03.txt (narration n11) and raw/L05.txt (narration n3). No board or publisher source consulted states who left whom.

findings.claim: When the National Theatre produced the play in 1994, it was the first time a Black British woman's play had been staged there (lesson 1); 'the 1994 National Theatre production was historic' (lesson 7).
findings.truth: Both dates circulate and neither is wrong enough to edit. The National Theatre production opened in December 1994 on tour and reached the Cottesloe in 1995; Wikipedia dates it 1995, Nick Hern's study guide says 1995. The significance claim itself is correct: the Bush Theatre calls Pinnock 'the first Black British woman to have a play produced at the National Theatre'.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Winsome Pinnock: 'premiered at Liverpool Playhouse Studio ... followed by a National Theatre production in 1995'; Bush Theatre 2018 production page. Recorded as a note on the sibling AQA unit too (F16).

findings.claim: She charges no fee for Enid's final reading, out of sympathy. (Flashcard: 'Nothing - she waives the fee out of sympathy.')
findings.truth: Not corroborated by any board, publisher or Oak resource consulted. It may be right, but nothing found supports it, and the sequence those sources do record is that Mai manoeuvres Del into taking the appointment with Enid. Left unedited; worth a look against the text if anyone has a copy.
findings.evidence: Absent from the WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, the Nick Hern study guide Scene Eight summary and the Oak Scene Eight lesson. Same note on the sibling AQA unit (F17).

findings.claim: All 48 practice questions are labelled '20 marks - Whole Text Essay' or '20 marks - Extract Comparison', stamped [20 marks], with bands Top (17-20) / Mid (9-16) / Lower (1-8).
findings.truth: Correct for this board and left alone. The comparison prompts match part (a) - compare the printed extract with an unseen modern extract, 20 marks - and the whole-text essays match part (b), a related question on the studied text, 20 marks. The band ranges cover 1-20 with no gap or overlap, so no rescale is needed. The only cosmetic point is that the ladders use three bands rather than the five house bands; that is not a factual error and I have not touched it.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md, section 3a (two-part question, 40 marks for Section A); question wording checked against every one of the 48 items.

summary: Fifteen real errors across all eight lessons, plus six notes. The unit was generated from the same broken template as the AQA Leave Taking unit, so most content errors repeat there; the exam errors are OCR-specific. The worst are: the play placed in either examined component when it sits only in the modern prose or drama section; the exam described as 'an extract with questions, or the whole play' when it is one compulsory two-part question, 20 plus 20, closed text, with no spelling and punctuation marks; Enid said to speak standard English when she speaks Jamaican patois throughout, which corrupts a whole lesson, its answer keys and two mark schemes; Scene 5 placed at Enid's house when Del is already living at Mai's; a fabricated Scene 6 palm reading and long-journey prediction; the mother's death reported by letter when it comes by telephone; Mai described as dying when she does not die; the play dated to 1984 with a knowledge check that marked the defensible answer wrong; and a one-word misquotation of the unit's most quotable line. 85 surgical edits written. Two items need a judgement call (Enid's job title, and who ended her marriage) and two lesson titles say 'Act 1' and 'Act 2' in a play that has neither.
